chem_ocra.11.0.summary: Analysing chemical reactions requires definitive, qualitative gas tests to prove the identity of evolved products. This revision guide covers the precise execution, expected observations, and underlying chemical reactions for identifying oxygen, hydrogen, carbon dioxide, and chlorine gases. Mastering these tests, including the correct equipment and safety precautions, is essential for securing top marks in OCR GCSE Chemistry practical and analytical assessments.

core.p: Chemical analysis often produces gases as by-products. To identify these gases, chemists use specific, reliable chemical tests that produce unmistakable visual or physical observations.
bullets: Gas tests rely on unique chemical or physical properties of the gas.
Tests must be carried out swiftly before the gas escapes from the reaction vessel.
Always use clean, uncontaminated equipment to avoid false positive results.
A positive test requires a distinct, unambiguous observation noted by the mark scheme.

callouts.p: Never rely on colour or smell alone to identify a gas, as many are colourless and odourless. Always use the specified chemical test.

core.p: Oxygen supports combustion vigorously. When present in sufficient concentration, it will cause a glowing splint to relight.
bullets: Reagent: A glowing wooden splint.
Method: Light a wooden splint, blow out the flame so the end is glowing red-hot, and insert it into the test tube containing the gas.
Positive Observation: The glowing splint relights with a bright flame.
Explanation: Oxygen gas is an oxidising agent that increases the rate of combustion of the glowing carbon on the splint.

callouts.p: A glowing splint relights in the presence of oxygen.
Do not state that a burning splint burns brighter. The mark scheme explicitly requires a glowing splint to relight.

core.p: Hydrogen is an extremely flammable gas that reacts explosively with oxygen when ignited in a confined space.
bullets: Reagent: A burning wooden splint.
Method: Hold a lighted wooden splint near the open mouth of the test tube containing the gas.
Positive Observation: A squeaky pop sound is heard.
Explanation: The hydrogen burns rapidly in air, producing water vapour and releasing energy as a sound wave: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O.

callouts.p: A lighted splint gives a squeaky pop when placed near hydrogen gas.
Always write 'squeaky pop' or 'pops with a squeak'. Simply saying 'it pops' is often insufficient.

fig.cap: Testing for hydrogen by applying a lighted splint to the mouth of the test tube.

core.p: Carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide solution (limewater) to form an insoluble white precipitate of calcium carbonate.
bullets: Reagent: Aqueous calcium hydroxide, commonly known as limewater.
Method: Bubble the unknown gas through a test tube containing clear limewater using a delivery tube, or draw it up with a pipette.
Positive Observation: The limewater turns cloudy or milky.
Explanation: Insoluble calcium carbonate forms: Ca(OH)2 (aq) + CO2 (g) -> CaCO3 (s) + H2O (l).

callouts.p: Limewater turns cloudy when carbon dioxide is bubbled through it.
If excess carbon dioxide is bubbled through limewater, the white precipitate dissolves to form soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate, turning it clear again.

fig.cap: Bubbling carbon dioxide gas through limewater to produce a cloudy white suspension.

core.p: Chlorine is a toxic, pale green gas that acts as a strong bleaching agent due to its reactivity with moisture.
bullets: Reagent: Damp blue litmus paper.
Method: Hold a strip of damp blue litmus paper over the mouth of the test tube or container holding the gas.
Positive Observation: The litmus paper is first turned red (due to acidic hydrogen chloride formed with water), and is then bleached white.
Explanation: Chlorine dissolves in water to form acidic solutions and hypochlorous acid (HClO), which destroys dye molecules.

callouts.p: Damp blue litmus paper turns red and is then bleached white.
You must specify that the litmus paper is **damp**. Dry litmus paper will not react with chlorine gas.

fig.cap: Damp blue litmus paper turning red then white in chlorine gas.

core.p: A quick-reference guide linking each gas to its reagent and positive test observation.
bullets: Review this table regularly to avoid confusing reagents and observations.
Ensure all test conditions (such as 'damp' or 'glowing') are memorised.

callouts.p: Examiners award marks only when both the correct reagent and precise observation are stated.

core.p: Gases produced in school laboratories can be toxic, corrosive, or flammable, requiring strict adherence to health and safety guidelines.
bullets: Chlorine gas is toxic and corrosive; tests involving chlorine must be performed inside a functioning fume cupboard.
Hydrogen and oxygen form explosive mixtures; keep quantities small and use safety screens.
Wear eye protection (safety goggles) at all times when handling acids, limewater, and generating gases.
Ensure good laboratory ventilation during any gas preparation practical.

callouts.p: Never inhale chlorine gas directly; always waft vapours gently toward your nose if odour is required, though standard tests rely on litmus.

core.h: Practical Setup: Generating and Collecting Gases
core.p: Before testing a gas, it must be collected safely from the reaction mixture using appropriate apparatus.
bullets: Insoluble or sparingly soluble gases (like H2 and O2) are collected over water in a trough using a measuring cylinder or test tube.
Denser-than-air gases (like CO2 and Cl2) can be collected by downward delivery (upward displacement of air).
Lighter-than-air gases (like H2) can be collected by upward delivery (downward displacement of air).
Delivery tubes must form an airtight seal with the reaction vessel to prevent gas loss.

callouts.p: Choose the collection method based on the gas density relative to air (average Mr approx 29).

core.p: Students frequently lose marks by confusing tests, omitting vital preparation details, or using imprecise terminology.
bullets: Confusing the oxygen test (glowing splint) with the hydrogen test (burning splint).
Forgetting to wet the blue litmus paper when testing for chlorine.
Stating that limewater 'turns white' instead of 'turns cloudy' or 'milky'.
Saying a burning splint 'goes pop' for hydrogen instead of a 'squeaky pop'.

callouts.p: Examiner mark schemes are exceptionally strict on exact wording. Memorise standard phrasing word for word.

core.p: Questions on gas tests often form part of larger experimental design or identification scenarios in Paper 2.
bullets: Step 1: Identify what is added to what (reagents).
Step 2: State the observation clearly (what you see, hear, or smell).
Step 3: Deduce the identity of the gas from the observation.
Step 4: Check if a balanced chemical equation is requested.

callouts.p: Look for 'Describe the test for...' vs 'Explain how you would identify...'. Both require reagent and observation.

analogy.p: Imagine a detective at a crime scene matching unique fingerprints to suspects. Each gas in chemistry has a distinct 'fingerprint reaction'—a unique reagent that reacts in a way no other gas does. For instance, hydrogen's fingerprint is its acoustic reaction (the squeaky pop), while carbon dioxide's fingerprint is its physical transformation of clear liquid into milk. Where the analogy breaks down is that human fingerprints are unique to individuals, whereas gas tests identify entire categories of chemical substances rather than individual molecules.

terms.d: A wooden spill with its flame blown out, leaving a red-hot ember used to test for oxygen.
An aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2, used to test for carbon dioxide.
Paper stained with indicator dye, used to test for acidity, alkalinity, or bleaching gases like chlorine.
An insoluble solid formed in a solution during a chemical reaction.
The characteristic sound produced when hydrogen gas ignites explosively with air.
The process of removing colour from a dye, characteristic of chlorine gas.
A substance that accepts electrons or supports combustion, such as oxygen.
A method of collecting gases based on their density relative to air.
Chemistry procedures focused on identifying what substances are present, rather than measuring how much.
The opaque, cloudy appearance of limewater when calcium carbonate precipitate forms.
A ventilated enclosure used to safely handle toxic or corrosive gases and chemicals.
A substance used in a chemical reaction to detect, measure, or produce other substances.

mistakes.w: Using a burning splint to test for oxygen.
mistakes.r: You must use a glowing splint that relights.

mistakes.w: Using dry blue litmus paper for chlorine.
mistakes.r: The blue litmus paper must be damp to allow hydrogen chloride and hypochlorous acid to form.
Mark schemes require 'turns cloudy' or 'turns milky'.
The accepted term is a 'squeaky pop'.
Hydrogen = lighted splint (pop); Oxygen = glowing splint (relights).

mistakes.w: Writing 'lime water' as two separate words or confusing it with limewash.
mistakes.r: Use calcium hydroxide solution or limewater.

mistakes.w: Saying chlorine turns red and stays red.
mistakes.r: It turns red briefly before being bleached white.

exam.q: Describe the test to identify hydrogen gas.
model: It gives a squeaky pop sound
exam.tip: State both the equipment/reagent and the exact observation to gain both marks.

exam.q: A student tests a gas with a glowing splint and it relights. Name the gas.
exam.tip: Write either the name or the correct chemical formula.

exam.q: Describe how you would test a gas to show that it is carbon dioxide.
exam.tip: Mention limewater and the cloudy observation.

exam.q: Explain why damp blue litmus paper is used when testing for chlorine, rather than dry blue litmus paper.
model: Chlorine dissolves in water on the damp paper
To form acidic / bleaching compounds that turn it red and bleach it white
exam.tip: Water is necessary for chlorine to exhibit its bleaching properties.

exam.q: A colourless gas is produced during a metal-acid reaction. Outline a complete analytical procedure to prove whether the gas is hydrogen or oxygen.
model: Collect the gas in a test tube
Test 1: Insert a glowing splint; if it relights, the gas is oxygen
Test 2: Apply a lighted splint; if it gives a squeaky pop, the gas is hydrogen
State that only one test will be positive
exam.tip: Structure your answer clearly, covering both potential outcomes.

exam.q: Write the word equation for the reaction of carbon dioxide with limewater.
model: Calcium hydroxide + carbon dioxide -> calcium carbonate + water
exam.tip: Limewater is calcium hydroxide; the precipitate is calcium carbonate.

exam.q: State the observation when chlorine gas is bubbled through universal indicator solution.
exam.tip: Chlorine is both acidic and a bleaching agent.

exam.q: Give one safety precaution necessary when generating and testing chlorine gas in a school laboratory.
model: Use a fume cupboard / wear eye protection / avoid breathing fumes
exam.tip: Chlorine is toxic; a fume cupboard is the standard correct answer.

exam.q: Identify the gas produced when dilute hydrochloric acid reacts with marble chips (calcium carbonate), and describe its test.
exam.tip: Link the reaction knowledge from C1/C2 to the gas test in C4.

worked.q: A student investigates the thermal decomposition of copper carbonate. A green powder turns black and a colourless gas is evolved. Design a test to confirm the identity of the gas.
steps: Identify the expected gas from thermal decomposition of metal carbonates: carbon dioxide.
Select the appropriate chemical reagent: limewater (aqueous calcium hydroxide).
Describe the method: connect a delivery tube from the test tube and bubble the gas through limewater.
State the positive result: limewater turns cloudy or milky due to the formation of solid calcium carbonate.
worked.ans: Bubble the gas through limewater; the limewater turns milky, confirming carbon dioxide.

worked.q: During electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution (brine), a greenish-yellow gas is evolved at the anode. Describe the test to confirm this gas.
steps: Identify the gas from brine electrolysis at the anode: chlorine gas.
Select the correct test material: damp blue litmus paper.
State the precise observation sequence: litmus paper turns red, then is bleached white.
Conclude that the presence of the bleaching action confirms chlorine.
worked.ans: Hold damp blue litmus paper in the gas; it turns red and is then bleached white.
